ta-l1d14q2-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph asking what the temporal procession consists in. Two questions are posed: whether in the temporal procession the Spirit himself is given, or only his gifts, or both; and, if both, by which gifts the Spirit is said to be given or to proceed temporally.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3515.summary: First argument that the Spirit himself does not proceed or is not given temporally. What is everywhere in itself does not proceed anywhere in itself, and the Spirit, being God, is everywhere.
claims: What is everywhere cannot proceed anywhere in itself.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3518.summary: Presses the point. If the Spirit comes to be in someone in a new way, that still supports the objection: God relates in the same way to all things, though not all relate to him in the same way (Dionysius, Liber de causis), and the diversity lies in the different perfections creatures receive. So the Spirit's being in someone in a new way means only that the person receives a new effect, and the whole giving or procession refers to the gifts, not to the Spirit himself.
claims: God relates to all things uniformly; diversity lies in the effects creatures receive.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3521.summary: Third argument. The temporal procession adds nothing real to the eternal on the side of the one proceeding (q. 1, a. 2), and by the eternal procession the Spirit does not proceed into any creature. So by the temporal procession he proceeds into creatures not on his own side but only in his gifts.
claims: The temporal procession adds nothing real on the Spirit's side.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3524.summary: Fourth argument. Infused virtue is no less sufficient for meritorious works than acquired virtue is for political ones, and acquired virtue sufficiently directs a person in all civil matters. So the Spirit himself need not be given with infused virtue; either the Spirit alone or the virtue alone suffices.
claims: Infused virtue suffices for meritorious works as acquired virtue does for civil ones.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3528.summary: Sed contra from Romans 5:5: the charity of God is poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to us. So both are given.
claims: Both charity and the Spirit himself are given.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3534.summary: Second sed contra. Love has the character of first gift, since in it everything is freely conferred. The Spirit is love and so has the character of gift, which he has only because he is given.
claims: The Spirit as love is the first gift and is given.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3543.summary: A further question: if both are given, which is given first? It seems the Spirit, through whom the others are given and who is the first gift.
claims: The Spirit is given first, as the one through whom gifts are given.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3546.summary: Contrary argument that the gifts are given first. They dispose us to have the Spirit, and a disposition is prior to what it disposes for.
claims: Dispositions precede what they dispose for.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3555.summary: Thomas's determination: the Spirit himself proceeds temporally, or is given, and not only his gifts. Considered on the side of its source, the procession is undoubtedly of the Spirit himself. Considered as related to that into which it proceeds, the relation is posited in the Spirit not because he is really related but because another is related to him. In receiving his gifts our relation does not terminate only in the gifts, as though we had only them, but also in the Spirit, since we have him otherwise than before. So not only his gifts but he himself proceeds into us, for he is said to be related to us as we are related to him. Both he and his gifts proceed into us: we receive his gifts, and through them we stand differently toward him, as by them we are joined to the Spirit, or he to us, assimilating us to himself by the gift.
claims: The Holy Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given in the temporal procession.
Our relation through the gifts terminates in the Spirit himself, so he is truly had by us.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3558.summary: Reply to the first argument. God's being everywhere implies a relation of God to the creature that is really in the creature, not in God. Such relations can be diversified on the creature's side by the different effects by which it is likened to God, so God is signified as standing differently toward it. So the Spirit, everywhere by the creature's relation to him, can be said to be newly in someone by that creature's new relation to him.
claims: The Spirit is newly in someone by the creature's new relation to him, though he is everywhere.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3561.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although the new mode of relation is diversified by the different gifts received, the creature's relation does not stop at the gifts but tends further to the one through whom they are given. So we can say that we have the Spirit in another way and that he is had by us differently, which is what is meant by saying he himself proceeds into us or is given to us.
claims: The creature's relation passes through the gifts to the Spirit himself.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3564.summary: Reply to the third argument. The Spirit is not said to proceed into us because something happens in him, but because, since we stand differently toward him, he can be signified as standing in another relation to us. He proceeds into us as to the relation that procession implies to that into which it is, though not as to the relation it implies to its source.
claims: The Spirit proceeds into us by a relation to his object, not by any change in him.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3568.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Infused virtue is far more sufficient than acquired virtue, and by its perfection it joins us most closely to God and likens us to him, and by that union a new relation to God arises in us. So the more sufficient it is, the more the Spirit is said to proceed in it and with it. Whether a created gift must be given with the Spirit is treated in Distinction 18.
claims: The perfection of infused virtue lies in joining us to God, and so the Spirit proceeds with it.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3571.summary: Concedes the two sed contra arguments.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3581.summary: Reply to the further question. The natural order of things can be considered in two ways. On the side of the recipient or matter, the disposition is prior to what it disposes for, so we receive the gifts of the Spirit before the Spirit himself, since we are likened to him by the gifts received. On the side of the agent and end, what is nearer to the end and agent is prior, so we receive the Spirit before his gifts, since the Son too gave us everything else through his love. This is to be prior simply.
claims: On the side of the recipient, gifts come first; on the side of agent and end, the Spirit is given first, and this is priority simply.
concepts: order of material and final causality

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3594.summary: First argument that the temporal procession concerns all gifts. Every gift to creatures proceeds from the liberality of the divine will, and the reason of liberal giving is love, so the Spirit is given in every gift.
claims: All gifts proceed from love as the reason of liberality.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3597.summary: Second argument. In any gift the creature acquires a new relation to God, being likened to him by participating a newly received perfection. That was what the Spirit's temporal procession meant, so he would be sent by natural gifts too, not only by sanctifying ones.
claims: Every gift establishes a new relation of likeness to God.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3600.summary: Third argument. According to Augustine, to be sent is to be known to be from another, and without sanctifying grace one can know by unformed faith that the Spirit is from another.
claims: To be sent is to be known as from another.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3604.summary: Fourth argument. Rabanus says the Spirit was given to the apostles to work miracles, and that gift is not sanctifying but freely given (gratis datum).
claims: The Spirit was given to the apostles for miracles.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3607.summary: Sed contra from Wisdom 1:5: the holy spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful. Whoever lacks sanctifying grace counts as deceitful, so the Spirit proceeds into no such person.
claims: The Spirit flees whoever lacks sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3613.summary: Second sed contra. The Spirit proceeds only into one in whom God dwells as in his temple, since by the Spirit one becomes God's temple (1 Cor. 6), and God dwells in someone only by sanctifying grace.
claims: God dwells in someone only by sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3616.summary: Thomas's determination. In the going out of creatures from the first principle there is a kind of circle or return, since all things return as to their end to that from which they came forth as from a principle. So the return to the end must be through the same things as the going out from the principle. As the procession of persons is the reason of creatures' production from the first principle, it is also the reason of their return to the end: through Son and Spirit we were made and through them we are joined to our last end (Augustine: the principle to which we return, the form we follow, the grace by which we are reconciled; Hilary: we refer all things through the Son to the one beginning). So the procession of persons into creatures can be considered as the reason of going out from the principle, in natural gifts by which we subsist, as Dionysius speaks of divine wisdom or goodness proceeding into creatures, which is not discussed here. Or it can be considered as the reason of returning to the end, only in gifts that join us proximately to our last end, God, namely sanctifying grace and glory, which is what is discussed here. As in natural generation the begotten is joined to the begetter in likeness of species only at the end of generation, so in participating divine goodness there is immediate union with God not by the first effects by which we subsist in natural being but by the last, by which we cling to our end. So the Spirit is given only in sanctifying gifts.
claims: The going out of creatures from God and their return to him follow the same processions of the persons.
The Spirit is given, in the strict sense, only through gifts that join us immediately to God as end: sanctifying grace and glory.
Natural gifts reflect the processions as the reason of going out, not of return.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3631.summary: Reply to the first argument. Great liberality is shown in natural gifts and freely given graces, but the perfection of liberality lies in gifts that join us to our final perfection, which order us immediately to the end. So the Spirit's procession is found chiefly in these.
claims: The perfection of liberality is in gifts that join us to the end.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3634.summary: Reply to the second argument. In the procession as discussed here, which includes the giving of the Spirit, any new relation of the creature to God does not suffice. The creature must be related to him as to something had, since what is given to someone is in some way had by them. A divine person can be had by us only for perfect fruition, by the gift of glory, or for imperfect fruition, by sanctifying grace, or rather as that by which we are joined to what we enjoy. The divine persons, by a kind of sealing of themselves in our souls, leave gifts by which we formally enjoy, love and wisdom; that is why the Spirit is called the pledge of our inheritance.
claims: Mission requires that the divine person be 'had' by the creature, through glory or sanctifying grace.
The persons seal themselves in the soul by gifts of love and wisdom by which we enjoy them.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3638.summary: Reply to the third argument. Not every knowledge suffices for mission, only knowledge received from a gift appropriated to the person, by which union with God is effected in us in the manner proper to that person, by love when the Spirit is given. This knowledge is quasi-experiential.
claims: The knowledge involved in mission is a quasi-experiential knowledge through an appropriated gift.

ta-l1d14q2-d1e3641.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The working of miracles is not a sanctifying gift, but it can be conferred with one. Since the apostles did not receive this gift without sanctifying grace, they are said to have received the Spirit temporally in its conferral.
claims: Freely given graces accompany the Spirit's mission only together with sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3510.summary: Sub-question 1 states arguments that only the Spirit's gifts are given, from his omnipresence, God's uniform relation to creatures, the temporal procession's adding nothing real, and the sufficiency of infused virtue, against Romans 5:5 and the Spirit's character as first gift.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3538.summary: Sub-question 2 asks whether the Spirit or his gifts are given first, weighing the Spirit as first gift against the gifts as dispositions.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3550.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 1 holds that the Spirit himself is given, not only his gifts. Our relation established through the gifts terminates in the Spirit himself, whom we thus have in a new way, and he is related to us as we are related to him. His new presence, despite his omnipresence, consists in the creature's new relation to him. The perfection of infused virtue lies in uniting us to God, so the Spirit proceeds with it.
claims: The Holy Spirit himself is given, as our relation through his gifts terminates in him.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3576.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 2 holds that on the side of the recipient the gifts come first, as dispositions, but on the side of agent and end, which is priority simply, the Spirit is given first.
claims: The Spirit is given before his gifts, simply speaking.
concepts: order of material and final causality

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 asks what the temporal procession consists in: whether the Spirit himself or only his gifts are given, and by which gifts.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Spirit himself is given in his temporal procession, and in what order with his gifts. Thomas holds that both are given. Through the gifts our relation terminates in the Spirit himself, who is newly had by us without any change in him. Simply speaking, the Spirit is given before his gifts, though the gifts dispose us for him.
claims: The Spirit himself and his gifts are given, the Spirit first simply speaking.

ta-l1d14q2-Dd1e3586.summary: Article 2 asks by which gifts the Spirit is given. Within an exitus–reditus framework, Thomas holds that the processions of the persons are the reason both of creatures' going out from God, through natural gifts, and of their return to him. The Spirit's mission in the strict sense concerns the return: it is given only through gifts that join us immediately to God as end, sanctifying grace and glory. Mission requires that the person be 'had', through gifts of love and wisdom that seal the persons in the soul, with a quasi-experiential knowledge. Freely given graces such as miracles accompany mission only together with sanctifying grace.
claims: The Spirit is sent only through sanctifying grace and glory, which join us to God as end.
The processions of the persons are the reason of both the going out and the return of creatures.

ta-l1d14q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 14 asks what the Spirit's temporal procession consists in. Article 1 holds that the Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given. Our relation through the gifts terminates in him, so we have him in a new way without any change in him, and he is given first simply speaking, though the gifts dispose us for him. Article 2 places mission within the exitus–reditus of creation. The same processions of the persons that ground creatures' going out from God ground their return, and the Spirit is sent strictly only by gifts that join us immediately to God as end, sanctifying grace and glory. In these gifts the persons seal themselves in the soul and are known quasi-experientially.
claims: The Holy Spirit himself is given in his temporal procession, together with his gifts.
The Spirit is sent only through sanctifying grace and glory, the gifts of return to God.
The processions of the persons ground both the going out and the return of creatures.
